extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Canadian/Western history; readers interested in the Mounties, indigenous treaties, and frontier policy
extracted.subtask_description: A narrative historical chapter describing the early operations, diplomacy, and treaty-making role of the North-West Mounted Police in Western Canada (1870s–1890s), including policing practice, relations with Indigenous peoples, and institutional decisions. It records conduct norms and policy prescriptions observed or recommended in that period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary duty: protect the Indians (wards of the nation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first business of the Police was to thus protect the Indians who were the wards of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Police were to shield Indigenous communities from depredations (e.g., whisky-traders, robbers) and to promote their welfare; protection included law enforcement and preventing exploitation that threatened survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty process: conserve Indian rights and provide reserves/payments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a lower civilization is to be superseded without injustice, the Government must proceed by process of treaty: conserve the rights of the Indian and secure to them both a place of residence and means of subsistence by a system of reserves and money payments, and extinguish the Indian title to lands outside their reserves to enable settlers to enter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaty-making must balance settler access with protections for Indigenous rights—explicitly providing reserves and annuities while legally clearing other lands for settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Mounted Police as visible assurance in treaty diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The impressive scarlet uniform of the Police somehow came to be recognized by the Indians as a sign royal of friendship; the Governor linked the Police with the Queen's government when making treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a respectful, visible, disciplined police presence to build trust and assist civil authorities during treaty negotiations and to reinforce the government's good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrust Mounted Police with annual treaty payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Governor Laird urged that officers of the Mounted Police be entrusted to make the annual payments to the Indians under this treaty: 'The Indians have confidence in the Police...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where trust in civil agents is weak, use respected local officials (here, Police) to administer sensitive functions (money payments) to reduce friction and fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisive enforcement against whisky-trade and outlaw traders
rubrics_metrics.description: MacLeod struck a body blow at the liquor traffic: whisky was seized/poured out, robes confiscated, culprits fined or jailed — leading to 'the complete stoppage of the whisky trade throughout the whole of this section of the country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive, visible enforcement of harmful illicit trades (here, alcohol trafficking) is presented as necessary to protect vulnerable populations and restore public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers must share hardship; no 'carpet knights'
rubrics_metrics.description: MacLeod taught his officers that he would have no 'carpet knights,' who claim immunity from hardship because of their rank; men's quarters proceeded before officers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders are expected to set an example by sharing privation and ensuring subordinates' needs are prioritized, to maintain troop confidence and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise animal welfare in field logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: When shelter was limited, MacLeod decided not a single log of men's quarters should be laid until the horses are provided for, as well as a few sick men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In expeditionary/remote operations, ensure transport and pack animals are adequately sheltered and fed first to preserve mobility and mission capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative and local resourcefulness of detached officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Police, often miles from any superior, developed powers of resource and initiative—e.g., Walker acting independently to escort Commissioners and defuse threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empower distant officers with discretion and expect quick judgment calls; decentralised initiative is essential when communication is slow or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish strategic posts to maintain peace over vast territories
rubrics_metrics.description: Posts were established at many points (Fort Walsh, Fort MacLeod, Fort Calgary, Battleford, Carlton, etc.) to exercise oversight and keep the peace across the vast area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create permanent local presences (forts/posts) at strategic nodes to exert authority, provide services, and stabilise frontier regions until treaties and settlement change conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policing as diplomacy: patience, courage, and open diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere handful of officers and men of the Mounted Police, with endless patience, unflinching courage and consummate skill in open diplomacy, kept the peace in an area larger than several European kingdoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective frontier policing combines enforcement with diplomatic engagement; cultivate patient, courageous officers skilled in negotiation and cultural understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use respected interpreters and commissioners in treaty negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaty negotiations were conducted with capable interpreters (e.g., Peter Erasmus, Jerry Potts) and commissioners who knew the country (e.g., Laird, Christie, McKay, MacLeod).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select negotiators and interpreters with local knowledge, linguistic skill, and cultural credibility to ensure clear communication and reciprocal trust in treaty processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government responsiveness to local conditions and advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Local police made recommendations (e.g., to make Treaty Number Eight) and influenced government actions; reports from officers (e.g., MacLeod's reports) shaped policy like moving headquarters or establishing forts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central authorities should heed informed local reports and recommendations when planning administration and treaties for remote regions.
